cefrAlignment: C1: recognising distancing, cleft emphasis, understatement and irony from the words and the situation matches the C1 descriptors for implicit attitudes and for colloquial and idiomatic speech.
examFidelity: The IELTS Part 3 MCQs, the lecture MCQs and the TOEFL Listen and Choose a Response items (all with 4 replies) fit exams.ts. Every ironic item can be solved from a mismatch with the facts that follow, not from intonation.
fixes: The Learn examples used 'did wonders for our response rate' and 'Twice the fun', which were word for word the answers to Practice 1 Q1 and Q7. Replaced them with new irony examples.
The Learn TOEFL tip mentioned the jammed printer and the 'express' bus from ex4. Replaced them with neutral situations.
Ex1 item 2 repeated a Learn example exactly (the umbrella). Replaced it with a new ironic remark.

The brain-training lecture said both sides of the 2014 open-letter debate 'accepted' that marketing ran ahead of the science, which I could not verify. Rewrote it: one letter (2014) said the claims exceeded the evidence; a reply a few months later said critics had overlooked research; and in 2016 one company paid $2 million to settle a US consumer-protection complaint (the Lumosity FTC case). Rewrote ex3 Q5 and its explanation to test 'the field is hardly united'. This also removes the length clue from the old key.
openConcerns: TTS intonation is flat, so ironic remarks may sound sincere. All the items are solvable from the words and the context, but a human recording would be more natural.
The lecture is 365 words, longer than a real TOEFL Academic Talk (100–250). It is presented as a lecture, not labelled as a TOEFL Academic Talk.
learnerOutcome: Learners can tell when a speaker distances themselves from a claim, stresses a main point, plays something down or means the opposite, and can answer from the words and the situation rather than from tone.
